title: Six ways to write down the same evening

objectives.statement: Classify each statement in a clinical extract as a person's report, another person's report, direct observation, inference, classification, or causal explanation, and justify each decision by naming where the statement came from and what would check it.
Rewrite a record entry that has collapsed an inference or a causal explanation into a description, so that the description and the conclusion are separately visible and separately checkable.

State what a classification and a causal explanation each add to a record and what neither establishes, using evidence about agreement between clinicians and about a causal claim that remains under dispute.

scenes.title: Six sentences about the same forty minutes
scenes.contentHtml:
Six sentences about the same forty minutes

R. is 34 and works rotating night shifts in a warehouse. On a Tuesday evening R. spent forty minutes in a clinic room with someone whose job was to find out what had been happening. Six sentences from that conversation reached the record.

  1. R. said he wakes around four most mornings and cannot get back to sleep.
  2. R.'s partner said R. has not been himself since the winter.
  3. R. answered slowly and twice stopped mid-sentence, looking at the floor for several seconds.
  4. R. is having difficulty concentrating.
  5. The picture meets the requirements for a depressive episode.
  6. The night shifts wrecked R.'s sleep and the mood followed.

One person, one evening, six sentences. They can sit in a single paragraph with nothing marking them apart, and each one answers to a different test.

  1. Ask R. again, and keep the words R. used.
  2. Ask R.'s partner, and note which parts of R.'s life the partner actually sees.
  3. Only somebody else in the room at the time could have contradicted this, and forty minutes later there is nothing left to look at.
  4. Show what the sentence was drawn from and see whether it carries. The record does not say, so the test cannot be run.
  5. Hand the same information to a second clinician and see whether they land in the same category.
  6. Find evidence that tells this account apart from a rival one. No rival is named anywhere.

The fourth sentence is the interesting one. Nobody saw R. having difficulty concentrating. Somebody heard R. answer slowly, watched R. lose the thread twice, and drew a conclusion. Written in that form, the conclusion looks like something that was noticed.

Why this is the method lesson

Psychiatry reaches most of what it studies through what a person says and through how they say it. There is no reading to take instead. What an examiner registers in the room is mostly expressive: speech, movement, facial expression, how easily a conversation gets going. Reading those takes much the same interpretive work as listening to an account.

General medicine has a fairly clean split between a symptom, which the patient reports, and a sign, which the examiner finds. A swollen ankle is a sign whatever the patient says about it. Psychiatry cannot copy that split cleanly, so it has to be careful about a different one: the difference between what was said, what was seen, and what was concluded.

A record that keeps those apart lets a later reader go back to the description and ask a new question of it. A record that merges them keeps only the conclusion, and a conclusion cannot be re-examined by anyone who no longer has the material it was drawn from.

Six categories have to stay apart: a person's report, another person's report, direct observation, inference, classification, and causal explanation. The first three are description. The fourth is inference. The last two are most of what people mean when they say interpretation. Every later lesson in this block runs on this sort, so it is worth getting slow and exact about it once.

What you will be able to do

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • take each statement in a clinical extract, say which of the six kinds it is, and name what would check it;
  • rewrite an entry that has buried a conclusion inside a description, so that both are visible and both can be questioned;
  • say what a classification and a causal explanation each add to a record, and what neither of them settles.

You need PSY-WEL-001. Two words used here, inference and model, are already defined in the premed course; both are explained again as they come up, so you do not need to have taken it. Every case is fictional, no personal disclosure is asked for, and you may answer in writing, by speech-to-text, in a transcribed recording, or with a tutor.

Check
id check-starting-position

Write two short answers before reading on.

  1. PSY-WEL-001 said a lens is a question and not a cause. Which of the six sentences above does that warning apply to most directly, and why?
  2. Sentence 4 says R. is having difficulty concentrating. Write down what someone would have had to see or hear in order to write it.

Keep both answers. The second one comes back in the worked example.

Feedback. Sentence 6 is the one the warning is aimed at: it takes a question worth asking about night work and states it as a settled cause. Sentence 5 is a near miss, because a category can also be treated as more than a question, though it claims to explain nothing. Your second answer is doing the real work of this lesson. Slow answers, lost threads, a request to repeat a question: all of that is description. The sentence in the record is a conclusion drawn from it. If what you wrote down was "R. said he cannot follow things at the moment", you have found something better still, because in that case sentence 4 is not a conclusion at all, and the wording gives a reader no way to tell.

Callout
id callout-teaching-boundary

Teaching example, not medical advice. R. is invented for this course and appears again in the lessons that follow. This lesson does not diagnose R., does not decide whether any impression recorded about R. is correct, and is not a procedure for assessing a real person. It stays with how statements are written down and what would check them.

Source Note

A methodological paper on the psychiatric interview supports the point that psychiatric phenomena are reached through a person's account and through expressive behaviour, and that the symptom-and-sign separation borrowed from general medicine cannot be applied cleanly in this field. The paper argues a position within an active debate about interview method; the narrow point used here, about access, is not the contested part.

scenes.title: What each kind of statement commits you to
scenes.contentHtml:
What each kind of statement commits you to

Grammar will not sort these for you. "R. is exhausted", "R. looks exhausted" and "R. says he is exhausted" have almost the same shape and three different origins.

Two questions do the sorting, and they have to be asked together. Where did this come from? And what would have to happen for it to be shown wrong?

Kind Where it comes from What writing it commits you to What would check it
A person's report R. that R. said this, in something close to these words ask R. again; keep R.'s own wording
Another person's report an informant: someone who knows R. and is speaking about R. that this informant said this, from where they stand in R.'s life ask that informant; record who they are and what they get to see
Direct observation the interviewer's eyes and ears, inside one bounded stretch of time that this happened in the room during those minutes a second person who was present at the time
Inference none of the above; it is drawn from them that this follows from material already stated display the statements it rests on and see whether they carry it
Classification a published set of requirements that this picture meets the requirements of a named category apply the same guideline and see whether a second clinician reaches the same category
Causal explanation a model of how the parts act on one another that one thing is producing or maintaining another evidence that separates this account from a named rival

The bottom four rows are told apart by their checks. The top two share a check of the same shape and are told apart by their origin, because the check leads to a different person and which person you go to turns out to matter more than anything else on either row.

Sort claims, not sentences. A single sentence can carry two kinds at once, and several in this lesson do. When that happens the sentence gets two entries and two checks.

One thing the table cannot show. A clinical record also holds lines that are not statements about the person at all: a missing result, a phone number, the date of the next appointment. Those belong to none of the six, and one of them turns up in the worked example.

The two kinds of report

The first instinct when a person and an informant disagree is to treat the gap as an error and pick a winner. Across clinical research, the two accounts overlap only weakly. Where the overlap is expressed as a correlation, values around 0.2 to 0.4 are typical, on a scale where 1 would mean the two accounts rise and fall together exactly and 0 would mean they carry nothing in common. Low agreement is closer to the norm than to the exception.

Some of that gap is error. Much of it is information, because informants see different stretches of a life and behaviour genuinely differs across them.

Which account is closer to the mark depends on what is being described. For internal states that cannot be watched from outside, the person's own account carries more weight. For outwardly visible and evaluative characteristics, the informant's account carries more. R.'s partner is the better source for whether R. has stopped answering the phone. R. is the better source for what four in the morning feels like. A record that keeps only one of the two has thrown away the comparison, which is why these are two kinds and not one.

Write the source into the sentence. "R.'s partner said R. has not been himself since the winter" is a usable line. "R. has not been himself since the winter" is the same content with the vantage point deleted, and nobody can now tell whether to go back to R. or to the partner.

Observation, and how little of it there is

Direct observation is what happened between two people inside a bounded stretch of time, written so that another person in the room could have agreed or disagreed.

"R. paused for around five seconds before answering three of the questions" is an observation. "R. was slowed" sits on the edge, because slowed is a comparison and the record has not said with what: R.'s own usual pace, or people in general. Those are different claims and only one of them is available to somebody meeting R. for the first time. "R. is withdrawn" has left the category altogether; withdrawal is a pattern across weeks, and nobody watches a pattern across weeks in forty minutes.

The check on an observation is unusually strong and usually short-lived. Another person present at the time could have contradicted it. Once the appointment ends that check normally expires, so the wording chosen in the room is the only version anybody will ever have. The exception is an observation that leaves something behind: a pulse written into a chart, or a house that will still be cold next week. Where a trace survives, so does the check.

Inference

An inference is a conclusion drawn from statements already made. That is the same meaning the premed science-method lessons give the word: a conclusion drawn from observations and reasoning instead of something recorded directly. Those lessons also let interpretation stand in as a second name for it. Here interpretation is reserved for the last two rows, classification and causal explanation, so inference stays narrow and keeps a row of its own.

The check is to display the material. An inference with its material attached is an argument a colleague can take apart: they can accept the pauses and the slow answers and reject the conclusion, or add a fact that changes it. An inference whose material has been deleted is beyond reach. Nobody can get back to what it was built from, so nobody can do anything with it except believe it or ignore it.

Classification

"The picture meets the requirements for a depressive episode" is a statement about a rule set. It says that somebody compared this person's picture with a published description and found that it fits. It says nothing about what produced the picture, how it will move, or what would help.

The check on a classification is agreement between clinicians, and agreement can be measured. The usual measure is a kappa: the proportion of cases on which two independent raters assign the same category, adjusted downwards for the agreement that guessing alone would produce. A kappa of 1 means they always agree; a kappa of 0 means they agree no more often than chance would arrange.

In the World Health Organization's field study for the ICD-11 chapter on mental disorders, 339 clinicians assessed 1,806 patients across 28 sites in 13 countries. Two clinicians sat in on the same interview and then classified the person independently. Kappa ran from 0.45 for dysthymic disorder up to 0.88 for social anxiety disorder.

Those two numbers came from one study, one guideline and one design, and a record writes both categories in the same font. A reader holding a category name has no way of knowing which end of that range it sits at, which is worth saying out loud whenever the name is used to decide something.

Causal explanation

"The night shifts wrecked R.'s sleep and the mood followed" is the strongest of the six and usually has the least behind it.

It commits you to a model, which is the premed course's word for a representation that keeps some features and relationships, drops the rest, and explains within stated limits. The model inside this sentence is small: it picks night work and sleep, treats four months of R.'s life as background, and asserts a direction of travel. Say that out loud and the check becomes obvious. What would separate this from the account in which the sleep loss and the mood are both downstream of something else, or from the account in which four months of low mood made the night shifts unmanageable?

A causal explanation with no named rival has nothing to be checked against, so naming the rival is most of the work.

Check
id check-sort-three-lines

Cover the table. Here are three lines from three different fictional records. For each one, name the kind and the check, and say which words told you.

  1. "Sister says he has been spending money he does not have."
  2. "Tearful throughout."
  3. "Symptoms began after the redundancy."

Then answer: which of the three could still be tested a year from now, and which one has already run out of time?

Feedback. The first is an informant's report, checked by asking the sister, and says is the word that marks it; notice that the sister is well placed for this, since spending is visible from outside. The second is direct observation, checked by a second person who was in the room, and throughout dates it to the appointment. The third is a causal explanation, checked by evidence separating it from a rival, and after is doing the work: a sequence has been stated and a cause has been implied without either being argued. On the last question, the sister can be asked again a year from now, the redundancy question stays open and unanswered, and the tears are gone: nobody can go back into that room, and nothing was left behind.

Four sources sit behind this scene. A methodological paper on the psychiatric interview supports the point about expressive observation. A review of multi-informant assessment supports the size of the usual disagreement between a person and an informant and the argument that disagreement carries information about context; most of its evidence concerns children and adolescents, and it reports that the pattern persists into middle age. A study of personality pathology supports the asymmetry between what a person and an observer each know accurately, and was conducted in one population rather than across psychiatry. The ICD-11 field study supplies the agreement figures; both clinicians heard the same interview, so ordinary practice, where two clinicians take their own histories, would not be expected to agree better than this.

scenes.title: Twelve lines from R.'s note, sorted
scenes.contentHtml:
Twelve lines from R.'s note, sorted

Here is the note from R.'s first appointment, as a clinician might actually write it: short, telegraphic, and mixing all six kinds without marking any of them.

Worked Example
id worked-example-sorting-the-note

Your job is to assign each line to a kind, name the check that goes with it, and work out which lines a reader six months from now will be unable to do anything with.

  1. Four months of low mood and loss of interest.
  2. Wakes at 4am, does not return to sleep.
  3. Has stopped seeing friends.
  4. Partner: "not himself since February".
  5. Weight down about 6 kg, unintentional.
  6. Speech slow; pauses of several seconds before answering.
  7. Poor concentration.
  8. Alcohol most evenings, increased over the last two months, to help with sleep.
  9. Feels cold, constipated, tired beyond the sleep loss.
  10. No thyroid function result available.
  11. Sleep disturbance secondary to alcohol.
  12. Impression: depressive episode.

Start with what is missing. Twelve lines and one interviewer. The lines are all that survives; the forty minutes are gone. Nothing in the extract says which words were R.'s, which were the partner's, and which were the writer's, and recovering that is most of the task.

Sort by the check, not by the wording. Two lines with identical grammar can belong in different rows, and a line that reads like a plain fact can turn out to be a conclusion. So for each line, ask where it came from and what would have to happen to show it wrong. Two of the lines carry two kinds at once, and their rows say so.

Line Kind Check What it has lost
1 A person's report Ask R. again R.'s own words. Low mood and loss of interest are the writer's vocabulary, and asking again next month gets a fresh account, not the one R. gave that evening.
2 A person's report Ask R. again Nothing. Specific, dated, and answerable.
3 A person's report Ask R. again Only the explicit attribution, which a reader can safely supply here. In a note where the partner also spoke, that would be a real ambiguity.
4 Another person's report Ask the partner The partner's material. Not himself is the partner's own inference, and the note kept the conclusion without what produced it.
5 Two candidates and no way to choose None, until the note says which it was Its source. If R. was weighed, this is an observation made by whoever weighed him; if R. said so, it is a report. Unintentional can only have come from R.
6 Direct observation A second person in the room, at the time Nothing, and it is the only line whose check has already expired.
7 Inference Show the material Its attribution and its working. Line 6 is plainly part of what it was drawn from, and the note never says so, never says what else went into it, and never says whose conclusion it is.
8 A person's report, with R.'s own causal account attached to it Ask R. again Nothing. To help with sleep is R.'s explanation of R.'s drinking, and the line correctly marks it as R.'s.
9 A person's report Ask R. again Very little. Beyond the sleep loss is a comparison added by the writer, worth noticing and stated in the open.
10 None of the six Order the test Nothing. It records a gap, which is why the test can still be ordered.
11 A category word plus a causal explanation Two different checks, and neither is available The two descriptions it replaced, which are lines 2 and 8, and the rival it never names.
12 Classification A second clinician applying the same guideline, if the note says which guideline The requirements it was measured against, and any sense of how reproducible that category is.

Four lines deserve the extra minute, and a fifth will not sort at all.

Line 3 looks like the most factual line in the extract and is a report. The test is simple: who would you go to in order to check it? You would go to R. If the partner had said it, the same words would be an informant's report and would carry a different vantage point.

Line 4 has two layers and the note kept one. The partner said something, which is checkable by asking the partner. The partner also concluded something, and what the partner actually noticed has not been written anywhere. Ask the partner what changed in February and the line moves into usable territory.

Line 7 is the failure this lesson exists for. Some of its material did survive, in line 6, and nothing on the page joins them. The note gives a reader a conclusion and a description on consecutive lines with no stated relation between them, no indication of whose judgement the conclusion is, and no way to know what else fed it. Repairing that on the day costs a dozen words. Repairing it in six months is impossible, because only the writer ever knew what else went in.

Line 11 does two things in five words. Sleep disturbance replaces line 2, which was specific and dated, with a category word that has no published rule set behind it, so there is nothing for a second clinician to re-apply. Then secondary to asserts a direction: the drinking came first and the sleep followed. Those two words are the whole causal claim, and they are the reason the line is more dangerous than it looks. Line 8 has R.'s account of the same two things pointing the other way.

Line 5 is the one that will not sort. The note never says whether R. was weighed or whether R. said so, and a line that could be either is usable as neither. Failing to place a line is a legitimate result: it locates a defect in the note.

A note on what the sort does and does not decide. The sort is about the statement as written, not about whether it is true. Line 2 could be sorted correctly and still be wrong; line 7 could be sorted as an inference and still turn out to be a good one. Line 12 is an impression recorded by the writer, and whether it fits R. is work for a later lesson in this block.

Change one thing and sort again. Suppose line 4 read: Partner: R. has stopped answering the phone since February. The kind has not changed and the value has. The partner is now reporting something they are placed to see, which is where an informant's account carries more weight than the person's own. The original line asked the partner for a judgement about R.'s inner state, which is the direction in which R.'s own account carries more. Same category, same speaker, better evidence, because the vantage point changed.

Now change line 6 to R. was slowed. Still an observation by intent, and no longer checkable, because slowed compares R. with a baseline the note never states. The category survived the change; the check did not.

What survives. Ask which lines a reader can still work with six months from now.

Lines 2, 3, 8 and 9 can be re-asked of R., and the answers will still be about the same things. Line 4 can be re-asked of the partner. Line 10 names something nobody has done yet, so the test can still be ordered; nothing on the page says that line 9 is why it matters, and whoever reads the note next has to make that connection again. Line 6 is fixed forever and was written tightly enough to bear it.

Four lines have gone dead. Line 1 is re-askable but its wording is lost, so nobody will ever know how R. described the four months. Line 5 cannot be sorted at all. Line 7 has lost its attribution and everything that fed it except line 6. Line 11 has neither its descriptions nor its rival. Line 12 rests on all of them, and nothing in the note announces which four are gone.

One last question. Go back to the answer you kept in the first scene, where you wrote what someone would have had to see or hear to write "R. is having difficulty concentrating". Compare it with line 6, and notice how much of what you wrote is not in this note at all. Then: if you could rewrite exactly one line of this extract, which one recovers the most for a later reader, and what makes it worth more than the others?

A strong answer names line 7 or line 11 and explains the choice by what the rewrite restores. Rewriting line 7 as poor concentration, my judgement, from the pauses in line 6 gives the next reader an argument they can accept or reject. Rewriting line 11 as R. reports the drinking increased to help with sleep; whether the drinking or the early waking came first is not established restores two descriptions and admits that a direction was asserted without evidence. Choosing line 12 is a weaker answer, because the impression sits downstream of everything else: repair the material and the impression becomes checkable on its own.

Source Note

The note extract, its twelve lines, and R. are invented for this course. The three sources support only the general points used in the sort: that psychiatric material is reached through report and expressive behaviour, that a person and an informant commonly give different accounts without either being an error, and that which account is more accurate depends on whether the characteristic is internal or outwardly visible. The asymmetry evidence comes from research on personality, so it is a principle to reason with here and carries no measured effect size for clinical records.

scenes.title: Two shortcuts, and what they cost the next reader
scenes.contentHtml:
Two shortcuts, and what they cost the next reader

Check
id check-predict-the-shortcuts

Commit to an answer before reading on, in one line each.

  1. Rank the six kinds from strongest evidence to weakest, or say why they cannot be ranked.
  2. A colleague writes "poor concentration" and leaves the observation it came from three lines away, unlinked. Name one thing this costs, or say that it costs nothing.

Feedback on the ranking. If you wrote one, keep it beside you: the next section is the reply to it, and there are three separate objections. If you said the six cannot be ranked, write down your reason now, because most people find one of the three and the other two are the interesting ones. The second question is answered further down this scene.

The first shortcut: a ladder of reliability

Misconception
id misconception-reliability-ladder

The shortcut sounds like this: direct observation is the hard evidence, a person's report is soft because people are unreliable narrators of themselves, and an informant's account is hearsay at one remove. Rank them in that order and you have a rule for whose word to take.

The intuition is imported from the rest of medicine, where a ranking often does useful work, because a number off an analyser and a report of feeling weak really are different grades of evidence there. Three things stop it working here.

An observation's check usually dies with the appointment. Nobody can go back into that room. A report's check is alive for as long as the person is: R. can be asked again tomorrow, in different words, and the answer compared with the first one. On the criterion of what can still be tested, the supposedly softest category outlasts the supposedly hardest.

The ranking also gets the informant backwards. Which account is more accurate depends on what is being described. For outwardly visible behaviour, the person who watches R.'s week is better placed than R. For what four in the morning feels like, nobody is better placed than R. A fixed ranking has to be wrong for one of those.

And the ladder assumes that observation in psychiatry is a firmer kind of evidence than report. Most of what is registered in the room is expressive, so reading it takes the same interpretive work as listening to an account, and the boundary between watching and concluding is genuinely soft.

Replace the ladder with something more useful: the six are differently checkable, and each is strongest where its own check is available. That is why they are worth keeping apart, and why none of them is the good one.

Test the replacement on a new question. Suppose you want to know how much R. actually slept last Tuesday. R.'s report is available and re-askable, and R. was awake in the dark without a clock, which is not a good position from which to time anything. The partner's report can cover when the light went off and when R. got up. An observation from a clinic room on Thursday says nothing about Tuesday at all. The best-placed source changed as soon as the question changed, which no fixed ranking can do.

The second shortcut: the harmless summary

The second shortcut is the one with teeth. "Poor concentration" compresses an observation into two words, everyone reading it understands, and nothing seems lost.

Compression is not the problem. Detachment is. The compressed line does not sit beside the material it came from, does not say whose conclusion it is, and does not say what else went into it. Line 6 of R.'s note sits directly above it, and even at that distance nothing on the page says the two are related.

Two facts about records turn that into a durable problem. Clinical notes are largely made of earlier notes: in one study of 23,630 inpatient progress notes written by 460 clinicians at a single centre over eight months, 18% of the text in a typical note had been entered by hand, 46% was copied, and 36% was imported from elsewhere in the record. A line does not get read once and discarded. It gets carried, and each carry makes it look more like something that was established somewhere.

The second fact is about what a carried label does to a reader. Work on diagnostic overshadowing, the misattribution of physical symptoms to an existing mental illness, names the psychiatric history recorded in the chart as one of the things that predisposes a clinician to explain new symptoms by it. The label does not sit inertly in the file. It arrives before the patient does.

Put the two together and a two-word summary written on a Tuesday evening can be read as an established finding a year later, by someone who has no way of knowing that it was one person's conclusion drawn from a few pauses in a conversation.

The same line, written twice

Take line 7 from R.'s note and write it both ways.

A. Poor concentration.

B. Poor concentration, my judgement, from the pauses recorded above. R. did not raise concentration himself.

Version B is thirteen words longer and does three things A cannot. It marks the conclusion as one person's. It points at its material, so a reader can accept the pauses and reject the conclusion. And it records who raised concentration: the interviewer did, and R. never mentioned it, which is the kind of fact that changes what a later conversation opens with.

Both versions carry forward equally well, and only one of them can be argued with.

Check
id check-recheck-the-repair

A different fictional record contains this line, and nothing else about the observation:

Agitated.

Write the version B of it: the conclusion marked as somebody's, the material it rests on, and whether the person raised it themselves. You will have to invent the material, which is the point. Notice how much you had to supply that the original line did not contain, and that a real reader has no way to supply it.

Then answer: which of the six kinds is "agitated" as written, and which kind was it probably meant to be?

Feedback. Whatever you invented, whether pacing or a raised voice or an inability to stay seated, the original line contains none of it and a later reader cannot reconstruct it. This is the harder case than line 7, because line 7 at least left its material somewhere in the note. Here nothing was written down at all. As written, "agitated" is an inference with its material gone. It was probably meant as an observation, and it could have been one if it had named what was seen. Compare your prediction at the top of this scene: if you said the summary costs nothing, this is the cost.

Source Note

The repair of the first shortcut rests on a methodological paper about the psychiatric interview and on research into what a person and an observer each know accurately; that second study concerned personality characteristics, so it supplies a principle rather than a measured effect for clinical records. The note-composition figures come from one service at one American hospital over eight months in 2016, and other settings and record systems will differ. The concept analysis of diagnostic overshadowing names a recorded psychiatric history among the things that predispose a clinician to misattribute physical symptoms; it does not measure how often that happens.

scenes.title: The two that get believed hardest
scenes.contentHtml:
The two that get believed hardest

Four of the six kinds are modest about themselves: a report says who said it, an observation says when, and an inference written properly shows its working. The remaining two are the ones this lesson calls interpretation. They arrive with more authority than they have earned, and they arrive in the sentences that change what happens next.

One word to pin down first

Depressive episode has appeared twice already, in the first scene's fifth sentence and at the foot of R.'s note, and the word inside it does two jobs in English. In ordinary speech, depression means feeling low. In psychiatry it names a syndrome defined by a published set of requirements, which is a claim about a rule set and not a description of a mood. This lesson uses only the second sense.

Turn that test on R.'s note. Line 12 reads Impression: depressive episode, and Impression marks it as the writer's judgement without saying which guideline was applied or which requirements were met. A reader cannot tell whether the second sense was meant carefully or the first sense slipped into a category's clothing. That is worth catching, because a letter that slides has turned a mood into a category with nobody deciding to. The mood lessons later in this block take the technical sense apart properly.

What a classification is doing

A category name says one thing: someone compared this picture with a published set of requirements and found that it fits. That is genuinely useful. It lets two clinicians on different continents mean the same thing, it connects a person to a body of evidence about people described the same way, and in most systems it is what opens a door to a service.

It says nothing about what produced the picture, how it will move over the next year, or what will help. Those are separate questions with separate evidence, and a category name answers none of them by containing them.

The ICD-11 field-study kappas from the previous scene are the reason to keep saying so. Two clinicians hearing the same interview agreed at 0.45 for dysthymic disorder and 0.88 for social anxiety disorder, under one guideline and one design. A record writes both category names in the same font, and neither the record nor the reader carries the number that belongs to it. Those figures also came from specialist mental-health services in the participating countries. The same categories get applied in general practice, in emergency departments, and by clinicians who reach for them far less often.

What a causal explanation is doing

"The night shifts wrecked R.'s sleep and the mood followed" is the sentence a reader remembers, and the one with least behind it. The previous scene set out the small model inside it: night work and sleep selected, four months of R.'s life left as background, a direction asserted.

What the sentence adds is the reason it survives every compression. A cause is the only one of the six that tells a reader what to do next. A report invites another question, an observation invites a second observer, a classification invites a service; a cause invites an action, and it is the sentence a busy reader acts on.

What it does not settle is almost everything a reader will take from it: whether the association is real at all, whether it holds for this person or only on average, and whether removing the cause would change anything. None of those follows from writing the sentence down.

Comparing whole explanatory models against each other, biological against psychological against social, is the next outcome in this module and is not the work here. The work here comes first: recognising a causal sentence when you see one, and knowing that it owes you a rival and something that would tell the two apart.

A causal sentence that outran its evidence

The clearest illustration comes from outside the case note altogether: the sentence that depression is caused by a chemical imbalance, and specifically by low serotonin.

In 2022 a systematic umbrella review in Molecular Psychiatry, meaning a review that gathers up the existing reviews rather than the original studies, examined six lines of serotonin research. It reported no consistent evidence of an association between serotonin and depression, and no support for the claim that depression is caused by lowered serotonin activity or concentration. The same review cites surveys in which 80% or more of the general public believe it is established that depression is caused by a chemical imbalance.

In 2023 the same journal published a reply from a different group, who argued that the review had applied its methods inconsistently, reported the evidence selectively, and misread the brain-imaging studies, and who held that the serotonin system is implicated in depression.

The dispute is live and this lesson does not settle it. What the episode shows is the shape of the problem. A causal sentence reached near-universal public standing while the evidence behind it was under specialist dispute, and the places it travelled to, from a leaflet to a conversation to a letter, did not carry the dispute with it.

What to write instead

A causal explanation earns its place when it names three things: the model, the rival, and what would separate them.

Before. The night shifts wrecked R.'s sleep and the mood followed.

After. R. works rotating nights and reports waking at four and not returning to sleep. One reading is that the shift pattern disrupted the sleep and the mood followed. Against it: the low mood is recorded as four months old, and the drinking has increased over the last two months by R.'s own account to help with sleep, which could account for the early waking on its own. The note dates neither the shift change nor the onset of the early waking, and that dating is what would separate these.

The second version is longer and is doing something the first cannot: it can be wrong in a way a reader can find. It is also honest about the fact that the record does not yet contain what the question needs.

Check
id check-classify-the-authority

Three sentences from three different fictional records. For each, say which of the six kinds it is, and what would check it. One of them is two kinds in one sentence.

  1. "Meets requirements for generalised anxiety disorder."
  2. "Symptoms are driven by the housing situation."
  3. "Panic disorder, precipitated by the bereavement."

Then answer: which of the three could two clinicians disagree about while both applying the guideline correctly?

Feedback. The first is a classification, checked by a second clinician applying the same guideline. The second is a causal explanation, checked by evidence separating it from a rival, and it names no rival. The third is two kinds joined by one word: a classification and a causal explanation, whose checks have nothing in common even though they share a comma. The last question points at the first sentence and at the classification half of the third. Those are the statements a guideline governs, and a kappa of 0.45 is exactly what two clinicians applying one guideline correctly and landing apart looks like. Nobody is applying a guideline to the second sentence, so the question does not attach to it at all.

Source Note
claims claim-icd11-reliability-range, claim-serotonin-contested, claim-chemical-imbalance-beliefsources source-reed-icd11-reliability, source-moncrieff-serotonin, source-jauhar-serotonin

The agreement figures come from the ICD-11 developmental field study, in mental-health settings in 13 countries, using a design in which both clinicians heard the same interview. The serotonin dispute is given from both sides and from the same journal: the 2022 umbrella review and the 2023 reply that contests its methods and conclusions. This lesson takes no position on which reading is correct and uses the exchange only to show what a contested causal claim looks like while it is being contested. The survey figure for public belief is reported inside the umbrella review rather than measured by it.

scenes.title: Practice on a record you have not seen
scenes.contentHtml:
Practice on a record you have not seen

Three tasks, with the support falling away between them.

Callout
id callout-practice-boundary

T. is invented, and so is anything you write here. These tasks are about how a sentence is written down and what would check it. None of them is a method for interviewing a person, deciding what to ask, or judging anyone's state, and nothing below should be carried into a conversation with a real person.

Completion problem

A line reads:

Anxious in the interview.

Take it that you wrote the line, and complete the repair by filling the four blanks:

"Anxious in the interview" is: ______. What I actually saw or heard was: ______. The repaired line has two halves and two checks. The check on the material is ______, and the check on the conclusion is ______.

Then write the repaired line as one sentence.

Feedback. The first blank is an inference. The second has to contain something a second person in the room could have agreed or disagreed with: a shaking hand, a rate of speech, a question asked three times, an answer given before the question had finished. The third blank is another person present at the time, and that check has already expired. The fourth is different in kind: display the material and see whether it carries the conclusion, which anyone can still do from the page. A repaired line might read: Anxious in my judgement: spoke quickly throughout, asked twice whether the door was closed. If your second blank contained "seemed nervous", you have written a second inference where the material should be; try again with something a video would have caught.

Supported problem

T. is fictional, 58, a retired teacher, seen at home by a community team. Six lines from the visit:

  1. Daughter phoned: T. has not been out of the house for three weeks.
  2. T. says the tablets make her feel "like cotton wool".
  3. House cold; curtains closed; post unopened on the mat.
  4. Low mood, likely bereavement-related.
  5. Denies any thoughts of self-harm.
  6. Poor self-care.

For each line, name the kind and the check. Two of the six are genuinely arguable; find them and say what the argument is about. Then name the pair of lines where one is the material for the other and the note has not connected them.

Feedback. Line 1 is another person's report, checked by asking the daughter, and it asks her about exactly the kind of thing a family member is well placed to see. Worth also recording is how often she visits, because that sets what "three weeks" is based on.

Line 2 is a person's report and the strongest line in the extract, because it kept T.'s own words. "Like cotton wool" cannot be recovered from any paraphrase of it, and a paraphrase would have to guess whether she meant sedation, slowed thinking, or something about her body.

Line 3 is direct observation, and it is well written: cold, closed, unopened are all things a second visitor could have contradicted. It is also the kind of observation whose check does not expire on the day, because a cold house and unopened post are still there next week. Notice that the line stops before drawing anything from what it describes.

Line 4 is two moves at once. "Low mood" may be T.'s report or the writer's compression, and the note gives no way to tell, which is the first arguable line. "Likely bereavement-related" is a causal explanation with no rival named; the word likely signals uncertainty about the answer while leaving the question itself unexamined.

Line 5 is the second arguable one. It reports an answer to a question, so it belongs with a person's report, and the word denies is doing work that a record should not do quietly. Denial implies something there to be denied. The line records neither what was asked nor how T. answered. Asked directly about thoughts of self-harm; T. said no is the same information with the implication removed.

Line 6 is an inference, and its material is sitting three lines above it in line 3. The note contains both halves of an argument and never joins them, so a later reader sees a conclusion and a description and no stated relation between them.

If more than two of your six answers landed in the wrong row, go back to the table in What each kind of statement commits you to, cover the check column, and re-sort R.'s twelve lines before attempting the next task. The sort becomes a habit before it becomes a rule, and the habit is built on repetition against different records.

Independent problem

Invent a short fictional situation of your own, in two or three sentences, borrowing nothing from a real person's life. Then write eight lines of record about it that include at least one of each of the six kinds:

  • a person's report with the person's own words kept;
  • an informant's report with the vantage point named;
  • an observation tight enough for a second person to contradict;
  • an inference with its material pointed at and its owner named;
  • a line that names a category and is written so a reader can see it is a category and not a description;
  • a causal explanation with its rival named and something that would separate them.

Now hand your own eight lines to the checks:

  • for each line, name what you would do to test it;
  • find the line that will be least useful in a year, and say why;
  • find any line that is two kinds joined by a comma, and split it;
  • find any word that carries an implication you did not intend, as denies does;
  • for your category line, say what a reader still does not know about how reproducible that category is.

If every line passes, make it harder: write the version of your record that a hurried clinician would actually produce, then repair it. The compressed version is the one that gets written in real life, and the repair is the skill.

Source Note
claims claim-informant-discrepancy-normal, claim-vantage-point-asymmetrysources source-delosreyes-informants, source-carlson-asymmetry

T. and the six lines are invented for this lesson. Two sources support the reasoning applied to line 1: that a person and someone close to them commonly give different accounts without either being at fault, and that an informant's account carries more weight for outwardly visible behaviour while the person's own carries more for internal states. The second source studied personality characteristics, so it supports a principle for choosing whom to ask, not a figure for how much better either source is in a clinical record.

scenes.title: Transfer: nine words in an emergency department
scenes.contentHtml:
Transfer: nine words in an emergency department

The sort was built for a psychiatric first appointment. Take it somewhere else.

M. is fictional, 41, and arrives at an emergency department at two in the morning with abdominal pain. The triage entry reads:

Known anxiety disorder. Abdominal pain, likely functional. Obs stable.

Nine words. They will be the first thing every clinician who meets M. tonight reads, and in a busy department some of them will read nothing else before walking into the cubicle.

Do the sort first

Work through it before reading on. Name the kind of each of the four statements in that entry, and the check that goes with each.

Known anxiety disorder is a classification, and it is not this department's classification. It was made somewhere else, at some time, by someone the note does not name, and it has been carried here. Its check is a second clinician applying the same guideline, and nobody in this department is going to run that check tonight.

Abdominal pain is a person's report, and it is the reason M. is here. Its check is asking M., which is available immediately and costs nothing.

Likely functional is a causal explanation. It asserts that the pain is produced by something other than a disease process in the abdomen. Its check is evidence that separates it from a rival, and the rivals here are the physical causes of abdominal pain. The note does not name one, and no such evidence is in it.

Obs stable, meaning the routine observations of pulse, blood pressure, temperature and the rest, is a compressed observation. It is the exception the second scene named: the numbers behind it are stored elsewhere in the system, so its check has not expired.

What the sort changes

The problem is not that any of the four statements is false. Each of them may be exactly right. The problem is the order and the register: a classification made elsewhere sits in front of a report, and a causal explanation about tonight's pain has been written before anyone examined tonight's abdomen.

This is the shape of diagnostic overshadowing, which the fourth scene introduced. Work on the concept names a psychiatric history recorded in the chart as one of the things that predisposes a clinician towards that misattribution, and reports consequences that include worsening physical illness and death. The same work notes that people with mental illness die around a decade earlier than others, with most of that gap accounted for by physical disease such as heart disease and cancer; overshadowing is one contributor to that gap among several, and the size of its share is not established.

Notice also what the earlier scene predicted. Likely functional is three words, it is easy to carry, and every subsequent note that copies it makes it look more like a finding. Nothing in the copied version records that it was a guess made at triage before an examination.

The task

Rewrite the entry so that a clinician arriving at the cubicle at 3am gets the same information without the conclusion arriving first. Your rewrite should:

  • put M.'s report before anything else, in M.'s terms;
  • keep the psychiatric history and label it as past history, so it cannot be read as an account of tonight;
  • either delete the causal explanation or write it with its rival named;
  • say what would separate the two.

Then answer two questions. Which single word in the original does the most damage, and why? And what would you want the note to contain that the original does not mention at all?

Guidance after your attempt

A workable rewrite runs something like: Abdominal pain since around 10pm, described as constant and worse on movement. Past history of anxiety disorder, diagnosed elsewhere. Not yet examined. Observations stable. It is longer, and it leaves the question open for the person who has to answer it.

The word doing the most damage is likely. It has the texture of caution and the effect of a conclusion: it commits the writer to nothing while telling the reader what to expect. A note that said possible functional pain, abdomen not yet examined would be doing the opposite job with almost the same words.

The thing missing from the original is the examination, and after that, time. The original says nothing about when the pain started, and duration is the sort of description that later readers most often need and most often cannot recover.

What successful transfer looks like

You have transferred the model if you can take a record from a setting the lesson never described, sort it without the categories being announced, and say what each statement's check would be in that setting. The sort itself did not change between a psychiatric clinic and an emergency department. What changed is which check is cheap: in the clinic, asking again is easy and the observation window is gone; in the department, the observation is continuous and the classification came from a system nobody present has access to.

Source Note
claims claim-overshadowing, claim-notes-carry-copied-textsources source-hallyburton-overshadowing, source-wang-note-text

M. and the triage entry are invented for this lesson. A concept analysis of diagnostic overshadowing supports the definition, the naming of a charted psychiatric history as a predisposing factor, and the reported consequences, including the mortality gap it cites; that analysis synthesises a literature and does not itself measure how often overshadowing occurs or how much of the gap it explains. The point about a short line being carried forward rests on a single-centre study of note composition in an American hospital, which describes documentation practice there rather than in emergency departments generally.

scenes.title: Clinical wrap-up: one sentence in R.'s referral letter
scenes.contentHtml:
Clinical wrap-up: one sentence in R.'s referral letter

Callout
id callout-wrap-up-boundary

Teaching example, not medical advice. R. is invented, the letter is invented, and nothing here says what is happening to R. or what should be done about it. The general facts about thyroid disease below are sourced and are used to show why a description has to survive in a record; they are not a rule for interpreting anyone's symptoms.

Six weeks after the first appointment, a referral letter goes out. Two lines of R.'s note have been compressed into a single sentence, and a third line has not made the journey at all:

Fatigue and constipation secondary to depression.

Six words. Sort them with the tools from this lesson before reading on.

The sort

Fatigue and constipation began as line 9 of the note, which was a person's report and a good one: R. said he feels cold, constipated, and tired beyond what the sleep loss would explain. The letter has kept two of the three, dropped the cold, dropped R.'s comparison, and stripped the attribution. It now reads as a fact about R. Nothing marks it as something R. said.

Secondary to depression is a causal explanation, and it is doing what line 11 did with the alcohol: two words assert a direction and no rival is named.

Depression is a classification, imported from line 12 and now used as the explanation of something else.

And line 10, which recorded that no thyroid function result was available, has not been carried into the letter at all. It was the one line in the note that named something nobody had done yet, and it is the line that did not survive.

Why this particular loss matters

Fatigue, lethargy, cold intolerance, weight gain and constipation are the commonest symptoms of hypothyroidism in adults. They are also strikingly non-specific. A clinical review reports a study in which none of thirty-four hypothyroidism-related symptoms could identify who had the condition, and notes that 70% of people with normal thyroid function have one or more thyroid-associated complaints. That is why the diagnosis rests on measuring thyroid-stimulating hormone in blood and not on how convincing a history sounds.

Notice that R.'s weight went the other way. That is exactly the sort of detail a description keeps and an explanation drops, and it is not this lesson's business to say what it means. It is this lesson's business that it should still be legible to whoever asks.

Follow that through with the lesson's own machinery. A report of feeling cold and tired is compatible with several accounts, so the report on its own settles nothing in any direction. Its value lies entirely in being a report that somebody can still act on. The letter has converted it into an explanation, and an explanation cannot be acted on: nobody can order a test against secondary to depression.

This is the failure from the fourth scene arriving at its destination. The compression looked harmless, the letter will be copied forward, and the version that gets carried is the one with the description removed. It is also the shape of what the triage note did to M.: a psychiatric category placed in front of a physical complaint, with the complaint's description thinned out behind it.

Write the letter sentence properly

Three lines instead of one:

R. reports feeling cold, constipated, and tired beyond what the disrupted sleep would account for.

No thyroid function result is available.

Whether these physical features belong with the mood picture has not been established. They are recorded here as reported, because they are non-specific and a thyroid result would speak to them.

Nothing in that version is a claim about R. that the note could not support. It costs three lines and it leaves every question open to the next person, which is the entire point of writing a description down.

What this lesson does not do

It does not tell you what is happening with R., and it has not weighed one reading of this case against another. That work belongs to the mood differential and longitudinal course lesson later in this block.

What this lesson does is keep the weighing possible until that lesson arrives. A record that kept the descriptions separate from the conclusions can be re-opened. A record that merged them has decided the question by deleting the alternatives, and it did so without anybody noticing.

Reconstruct it

Close the lesson and complete these from memory.

  1. The six kinds are…
  2. The check on a person's report is…, and the check on an observation is…, and the difference between them is…
  3. An inference with its material deleted cannot be…
  4. A classification tells you…, and does not tell you…
  5. A causal explanation is not being checked at all unless…

Then take the sentence "fatigue and constipation secondary to depression" and say, in one line, what each of its three parts would have needed in order to be checkable.

Recovery route

Take the assessment attached to this lesson before looking back. Then use whichever of these applies.

  • If the six kinds do not come back, reread the table in What each kind of statement commits you to, cover it, and re-sort the three lines in that scene's prompt from memory.
  • If you can name the kinds but not the checks, work the twelve-line note again and fill in only the check column.
  • If the two reports keep collapsing into one, redo the change in the worked example where the partner's line becomes a report about the phone, and say why the same speaker produced better evidence.
  • If a classification and a causal explanation still feel like the same move, go back to the three fictional record sentences in The two that get believed hardest and name which words carry which claim.
  • If you can sort but cannot repair, do the completion problem again and write only the material line, with no conclusion attached to it.

Retake with a different fictional record. Sorting the same twelve lines a second time tests your memory of the answers rather than your grip on the method.

Accessibility and alternatives

This lesson is text-first, untimed, and asks for no personal health information. Every table restates its logic in the surrounding prose, and no distinction depends on colour, position, sound, motion, hover, or a timed reveal. You may respond by typing, by speech-to-text, in a transcribed recording, or in conversation with a tutor; what is assessed is the structure of your reasoning and never the medium. Where a prompt asks you to invent a record, a spoken or dictated version counts in full.

If any of this material lands close to a difficult personal experience, stop or leave without penalty. EmbeddedKnowledge does not monitor learners and provides no care. For personal help, use a qualified local service or your current emergency route.

What comes next

The next lessons in this block put the sort to work. Setting, role and consent decides what R. was told the conversation was for, which changes what R.'s report means. Mental-status observation takes the third row seriously and asks how to describe a person's state without shorthand that flattens them. Mood phenomenology assembles a picture out of the descriptions this lesson insisted on keeping. The differential lesson then asks what else the picture could be, and it can only do that because the descriptions are still there.

Source Note
claims claim-hypothyroid-features-nonspecific, claim-notes-carry-copied-text, claim-overshadowingsources source-chaker-hypothyroidism, source-wang-note-text, source-hallyburton-overshadowing

A clinical review of hypothyroidism supports the presenting features, their non-specificity, the finding that no single symptom identifies the condition, the figure for complaints among people with normal thyroid function, and the reliance on biochemical testing; it describes adults in general and is not a rule for any individual. The point that a compressed line gets carried forward rests on a single-centre study of note composition. The concept analysis of diagnostic overshadowing supports the pattern of a psychiatric record shaping how later physical complaints are read. R., the note, and the referral letter are invented for this course.

assessment.title: Sorting, repairing, and appraising clinical statements

items.prompt: For each of the five lines, name which of the six kinds it is and what would check it. Then answer two further questions: which of the six kinds does not appear in this extract at all, and which line is part of the material for another line while the record leaves them unconnected?
items.stimulus:
Five lines from the record of a fictional first appointment.

1. Brother says he has been sleeping in the car.
2. Speech quiet; answered in single words for the first ten minutes.
3. Says the flat he moved into last month "feels like it belongs to someone else".
4. Not managing at home.
5. Withdrawal driven by the recent move.

answer.correct: 1 is another person's report, checked by asking the brother, who is well placed to know where his brother sleeps. 2 is direct observation, checked by a second person present at the time, and that check has already expired. 3 is a person's report and keeps the person's own words, checked by asking again. 4 is an inference, checked by displaying the material it rests on. 5 is a causal explanation with no rival named, checked by evidence that separates it from a rival. No classification appears in the extract. Line 1 is part of the material for line 4, and nothing on the page connects them.
answer.summary: Sort five lines by origin and check; notice that classification is absent and that line 1 underwrites line 4 without being linked to it.
answer.reasoning: The item tests the sort on material the lesson never showed. Line 1 also exercises the vantage point, since where somebody sleeps is exactly what a family member is placed to observe. Line 2 is the only line whose check has expired. Line 4 repeats the failure the lesson is built around, in the form where the material survives on the page and the link does not, which is the pattern of lines 3 and 6 in the practice record. Line 5 uses the word 'driven' where R.'s note used 'secondary to', so a learner who attached the skill to a phrase rather than to a claim will miss it.
acceptableResponses: Naming line 3 as a second contributor to line 4's material is a stronger answer, not a wrong one, since it also describes how the person is living.
A response may argue that line 3 carries a small inference by the writer if it treats the quoted phrase as the person's report and says which words were added.
A response that notices line 5 explains a withdrawal that no line in the extract describes has found a real second defect and should be credited.
Equivalent wording for the checks is acceptable: 'go back and ask the brother', 'someone else who was in the room', 'show what it was drawn from', 'name what else it could be'.
commonErrors: Calling line 1 hearsay or ranking it below the person's own report, which reverses the vantage point for outwardly visible behaviour.
Calling line 4 an observation because it appears in a list of descriptions.
Calling line 5 an inference. It is an inference in the loose sense, and the lesson separates causal explanation because its check is different: it needs a named rival.
Missing that no classification appears, usually because line 5 mentions a cause and gets read as a diagnosis.

items.prompt: Which line is an inference written in the voice of a direct observation, with nothing left for a reader to check it against?

options.text: Paused for around eight seconds before answering.
Restless, my judgement: stood up twice and walked to the window mid-answer.
Partner says he has been checking the locks repeatedly.

answer.summary: 'Uncooperative during the assessment' is a conclusion written in the grammar of something that was watched, with no material and no owner.
answer.reasoning: Nobody sees uncooperativeness. It is drawn from short answers, refusals, lateness, or what a person declines to discuss, and the line records none of that; the word also carries a judgement about the person's intent that the record never argues for. The first option names a countable event a second person in the room could have contradicted. The third is also a conclusion, and it is the repaired form: it marks its owner and points at its material, so it is exactly what the disguised line should have looked like. The fourth marks its speaker.
commonErrors: Choosing the restless line because it contains a judgement word. A judgement is not the defect; a judgement with nothing attached to it is.
Choosing the partner's line because it is second-hand. Second-hand is a different problem from disguised, and that line states its source correctly.
Choosing the eight-second pause because the number looks like a judgement. A stated duration is exactly what makes it contradictable.

items.prompt: Rewrite the line "Guarded throughout the interview." so that the description and the conclusion are separately visible. Invent plausible material, mark the conclusion as your judgement, and then name the check on each half of your rewrite.

answer.correct: A rewrite that contains observable material a second person in the room could have contradicted, an explicitly attributed conclusion, and the two checks: another person present at the time for the description, and displaying the material for the inference. For example: 'Answered most questions in a few words and twice said he would rather not go into it; guarded, on my judgement.' The description's check expired at the end of the appointment; the inference's check is the material now attached to it.
answer.summary: Split the line into attached material and an attributed conclusion, and name a different check for each half.
answer.reasoning: The repair is the skill the lesson is for. Both halves are required: material with no conclusion leaves the reader to guess what the interviewer thought, and a conclusion with no material reproduces the original defect in longer words. Naming the two checks demonstrates that the halves are different kinds of statement rather than one statement written twice.
acceptableResponses: Any observable material is acceptable if a person in the room could have disagreed with it: length of answers, refusals to expand, delay, posture, where the person looked.
'On my judgement', 'my impression', 'I took this to mean' and similar all count as attribution.
A response that says the description's check has already expired earns full credit on that criterion; saying only 'another person present' is also acceptable.
commonErrors: Writing a second inference as the material, such as 'seemed reluctant' or 'was uncomfortable'. Neither is something a second person could have contradicted.
Attaching material but leaving the conclusion unattributed, so the reader still cannot tell whose judgement it is.
Naming one check for both halves, which loses the distinction the rewrite was made to expose.

items.prompt: Select every statement that is true of a diagnostic classification recorded in a letter.

options.text: It states that someone compared this picture with a published set of requirements and found that it fits.
It states what produced the picture.
Its reproducibility can be measured, and measured agreement between clinicians is far better for some categories than for others.
It states how the picture will change over the next year.
It supplies the rival account against which a causal claim in the same letter could be tested.
It connects the person to a body of evidence about people described the same way.

answer.summary: A classification reports a match against published requirements, carries a measurable and category-dependent level of agreement, and connects the person to evidence about similarly described people; it states neither a cause, nor a course, nor a rival.
answer.reasoning: The first option is what a category name actually asserts, and the last is why anyone bothers to write one. The agreement option is supported by the ICD-11 field study, where two clinicians hearing the same interview agreed at 0.45 for one category and 0.88 for another. Cause and course are separate questions answered by separate evidence, and a category name does not contain them. The rival option confuses the two kinds this scene separates: a classification cannot serve as the rival for a causal claim, because it is not a causal claim.
commonErrors: Selecting the cause option, which is the collapse the whole scene is about.
Selecting the course option because categories are often used to discuss prognosis; use is not the same as content.

Rejecting the evidence-connection option because it sounds like an over-claim. It is the modest and accurate statement of what a shared category buys, and rejecting every confident-sounding option is not the same as reading them.
Selecting only the first option and treating measured agreement as a technical detail rather than part of what the name carries.

items.prompt: Sort each part of this referral sentence and say what the sentence has lost. Then name which of the six kinds does not appear in it at all, and say what that absence costs. Rewrite it so that nothing is decided which the record cannot support, and finish by stating what a later reader could do with your version that they cannot do with the original.
items.stimulus: From a fictional referral letter about a different person: "Chest tightness and dizziness secondary to anxiety. Known panic disorder."

answer.correct: 'Chest tightness and dizziness' began as the person's report and has been stripped of its attribution and of the person's own wording. 'Secondary to anxiety' is a causal explanation with no rival named. 'Known panic disorder' is a classification made elsewhere, and it is being used here as the explanation of a physical complaint. Direct observation is the kind that does not appear at all: nothing in the sentence records that anybody examined this person or measured anything, so the one kind of statement that would bear on tonight is missing while three that do not are present. A workable rewrite restores the report and its attribution, records what is not known, and either removes the causal claim or writes it with its rival: for example, 'Reports chest tightness and dizziness, in these words, starting about a month ago. Past classification of panic disorder made elsewhere. Not examined; nothing recorded tonight. Whether these episodes belong with that history is not established.' A later reader can act on the rewrite: they can ask the person about the symptoms, examine and investigate, and see that a question was left open, none of which is possible against the original.
answer.summary: The sentence collapses a report, a causal explanation and an imported classification into nine words, contains no observation at all, and the repair restores the report, names what is unknown, and leaves the question open.
answer.reasoning: This is the wrap-up transferred to a different person and a different pair of symptoms, so it cannot be answered from memory of R.'s letter, and the absent-kind question has no counterpart in any scene. It requires the full sort, the repair, and the appraisal of both high-authority kinds. The strongest answers notice that a psychiatric classification is being used as the explanation of a physical complaint, which is the shape of diagnostic overshadowing, and that the loss is not merely stylistic: an explanation cannot be investigated, whereas a report can.
acceptableResponses: A rewrite that deletes the causal claim entirely is fully acceptable, provided the answer says why deleting it loses nothing that was checkable.
Naming informant report as a second absent kind is acceptable alongside direct observation, provided the answer says what an informant could have added here.
An answer may add that the duration of the symptoms is missing, that no examination is recorded, or that the origin and date of the panic disorder classification are unstated. Each is a genuine gap.
Naming the pattern as diagnostic overshadowing is credited but not required; describing the same mechanism in plain words earns the same marks.
commonErrors: Repairing only the wording and leaving 'secondary to' in place, so the causal claim survives the rewrite.
Treating 'known panic disorder' as description because it appears as background rather than as a conclusion.
Producing a longer sentence that is still one statement, instead of separating the parts so each can be checked on its own.
Answering what is wrong with the sentence without saying what a later reader gains, which is the part that shows the point was understood rather than the rule memorised.

criteria.description: Assigns the correct kind to each of the five lines.
Names a usable check for each line, including that the observation's check has expired.
Identifies that no classification appears, and that line 1 supplies part of the material for line 4.
Selects the line that carries a conclusion in the grammar of an observation.
Supplies material a second person in the room could have contradicted.
Keeps the conclusion and marks it as the writer's judgement.
Names a different check for each half of the rewrite.
Selects all three true statements: the match against published requirements, the measurable and category-dependent agreement, and the connection to evidence about similarly described people.
Excludes cause, course, and the claim that a classification supplies a rival account.
